questions.question: If a component declares `providers: [CartService]`, what happens when that component's children inject `CartService`?
options: They get the same root singleton as the rest of the app
They get a new instance scoped to that component and its subtree, separate from the root instance
Angular throws an error for redeclaring a provider
questions.explanation: A provider declared on a component creates a new injector for that subtree, so descendants resolve to that scoped instance instead of walking further up to root.

questions.question: What is an `InjectionToken` used for?
options: Only for injecting Angular's built-in services
Providing a unique, type-safe key for injecting values that aren't classes, like plain config objects
questions.explanation: Since a plain object or primitive can't be used as a DI token the way a class can, InjectionToken gives you a unique identifier to provide and inject non-class values.

questions.question: Which provider option lets you supply an already-constructed value directly, with no instantiation?
questions.explanation: useValue hands Angular a ready-made value to return whenever that token is injected — ideal for constants and configuration objects.

questions.question: Why is `useClass` particularly useful in testing?
options: It disables dependency injection during tests
It lets you swap in a fake/mock implementation under the same token, so components under test never need to know the difference
It only works in production builds
questions.explanation: By providing a FakeCartService under the CartService token in a test module, components that inject CartService transparently receive the fake instead.
